This post never publishes (`draft: true`). It exists so the theme can be
checked against real elements: running text, headings, inline `code`, code
blocks, a SAS and R pair, callouts, a figure, a table, margin notes and
footnotes. Preview it with `quarto preview` from `blog-src/`.

## Running text

Body text is Newsreader at 18 pixels with generous leading, set to a measure
near 68 characters. Headings, captions, tables and navigation use Atkinson
Hyperlegible Next, which was drawn for low-vision readers and keeps `l`, `1`
and `I` distinct, a useful property on a site full of variable names.[^fonts]

[^fonts]: Code uses Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono, from the same family, so code and
    prose share proportions.

A margin note sits beside the paragraph it annotates and drops inline on a
phone.

::: {.column-margin}
Margin notes suit asides that would otherwise break the argument: a citation,
a caveat, a version number.
:::

### A third-level heading

Links look [like this](https://ehrlinger.github.io/) and keep their underline,
since colour alone is not enough to mark them.

## Translating SAS to R

The SAS-to-R series will lean on this pattern: the same step in both languages,
one tab each.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## SAS

```sas
proc freq data=study.patients;
  tables sex*nyha / chisq;
run;
```

## R

```r
library(dplyr)

patients |>
  count(sex, nyha) |>                         # <1>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = nyha,
                     values_from = n)

chisq.test(table(patients$sex, patients$nyha)) # <2>
```

1. `count()` gives the cell counts that `PROC FREQ` prints as its table body.
2. The `/ chisq` option maps to a separate call; R keeps tabulation and testing apart.

:::

The `group="language"` attribute links every tabset on the page, so a reader
who picks R once sees R everywhere.
